data.title: 3 Apparel Stocks with a ‘Perfect 10’ Smart Score
data.description:
Gap (GAP), Ralph Lauren (RL), and Victoria’s Secret (VSXY) are three apparel stocks with a ‘Perfect 10’ Smart Score on TipRanks. This proprietary quantitative scoring system from TipRanks rates stocks on eight key market factors. The TipRanks Smart Score lets investors quickly analyze stocks based on Wall Street analyst ratings, fundamentals, technicals, news sentiment, and other market factors. The Top Smart Score Stocks tool helps to filter the leading stocks with a top score of 10 by market cap and sector.

With Black Friday kicking off the holiday shopping rush, retail stocks are back in focus. The National Retail Federation (NRF) projects U.S. winter holiday sales to top $1 trillion for the first time, predicting 4.2% year-over-year growth across November and December. Now that peak shopping season is underway, it’s a good time to take a closer look at these top-scoring apparel stocks. Let’s look at each of these three apparel stocks in more detail.

Is Gap Stock a Buy, According to Analysts?

Gap Inc. is a global apparel retailer operating Old Navy, Gap, Banana Republic, and Athleta across nearly 3,500 store locations and e-commerce channels in about 40 countries. In its Fiscal Q3 2026 report last week, the company posted 2% year-over-year net sales growth to $4.01 billion, while adjusted diluted earnings per share (EPS) jumped 32% to $0.82, topping estimates. Growth was led by its Gap label, where comparable sales rose 9% for the 12th straight quarter. Although management trimmed its full-year revenue outlook to roughly flat after warm weather in October and early November delayed demand for cold-weather apparel, company executives noted that sales rebounded once temperatures cooled.

On Wall Street, 20 analysts have covered GAP stock over the past three months, with eight rating it a Buy and 12 a Hold. The average GAP price target of $24.62 implies 6.06% upside from the last price of $23.21.

What Is the Price Target for Ralph Lauren?

Ralph Lauren is a global designer and marketer of premium lifestyle apparel, accessories, home goods, and fragrances across North America, Europe, and Asia. In its Fiscal Q2 2027 results reported earlier this month, net revenue climbed 9% year-over-year to $2.19 billion, fueled by a 28% revenue surge in Asia and 10% global direct-to-consumer comparable sales growth. Adjusted diluted EPS rose 22% year-over-year to $4.64. Management raised its full-year Fiscal 2027 constant-currency revenue growth outlook to 6%–7%. The company has a market cap of $23.49 billion.

Looking ahead, RL carries a Strong Buy consensus rating on Wall Street, with all nine analysts covering the stock rating it a Buy. The average RL price target of $457.44 implies 14.16% upside from the November 25 closing price of $400.71.

Is Victoria’s Secret a Good Stock to Buy?

Victoria’s Secret & Co. is a specialty retailer of intimate apparel, sleepwear, loungewear, and beauty products operating roughly 1,400 retail stores under the Victoria’s Secret, PINK, and Adore Me brands. In its Q2 2026 report in September, net sales rose 10% year-over-year to $1.61 billion on 9% comparable sales growth, while adjusted diluted EPS nearly tripled to $0.95. The company’s Q3 2026 earnings release is scheduled for December 3. It has a market cap of $7.45 billion.

VSXY has an average price target of $106.27, suggesting 16.09% upside from the last price of $91.54. The stock holds a Moderate Buy consensus on TipRanks, with six Buy and 11 Hold ratings.

data.title: Anthropic vs. Coinbase: One Stock Is Overhyped, One Is Oversold, Says Top Investor
data.description:
Crypto bulls spent the fall waiting for fresh money to find its way back to them. Some of it may have gone to the year’s most anticipated listing instead. Days before Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) made its Nasdaq debut on Nov. 19, an executive at Coinbase (NASDAQ:COIN) called the idea that AI IPOs are drawing risk capital away from bitcoin “a reasonable argument.”

Neither stock has had much to cheer about since. Anthropic closed below its $83 IPO price in the two sessions before Thanksgiving, then climbed above it ahead of Friday’s shortened session. Coinbase is also rising today, but sits near a three-year low, even as bitcoin heads for its first weekly gain in two months.

5-star investor Dilantha De Silva went through the numbers on both companies, and they led him to different places.

With Anthropic, De Silva starts with margins. The company counts only the cost of running its models for customers against revenue, while the cost of training new models goes under research and development. On that basis, its gross margin is about 85%. The investor isn’t convinced. Models released in the six months to Sept. 30 generated more than 80% of third-quarter revenue, which suggests each one earns most of its money for only a short time before it’s replaced. To him, that makes training an ongoing cost of doing business rather than a long-term investment. Counting all compute and infrastructure spending, roughly 57% of revenue in the first nine months, he puts the gross margin closer to 43%.

He has a similar issue with sales made through the cloud marketplaces run by Amazon, Google and Microsoft, which handled about 44% of revenue over those nine months. When a customer buys Claude this way, Anthropic counts the full price as revenue, even though the cloud provider keeps a cut. Those fees go under sales, marketing and partnerships instead, an expense line that grew to about 17% of revenue from around 13% a year earlier. In the investor’s view, that makes Anthropic’s revenue look larger than what it actually keeps.

Revenue per dollar of compute comes next. De Silva gives the company credit for the steep rise since early 2025, but the figure fell to 1.72x in Q3 from just over 2x in Q2. Compute costs climbed about 77% from the previous quarter while revenue rose 47%, partly because Anthropic spent $5 billion on costly short-term capacity. With about $71 billion in commitments due over the next 12 months, he expects more pressure.

Then there’s competition. With products like Claude Docs, Sheets and Meetings, Anthropic is now selling tools that compete with Microsoft’s and Google’s own office software, even though those two companies also sell a large share of Anthropic’s products through their cloud marketplaces. De Silva sees this expansion into business software as Anthropic’s best chance for growth, but it also risks upsetting the partners it depends on.

He doesn’t expect Anthropic to stumble, yet with a market cap of about $1.1 trillion, he thinks the stock leaves little room for error.

Bottom line, De Silva rates ANT a Hold. (To watch De Silva’s track record, click here)

Turning to Coinbase, subscription and services made up 49% of net revenue in Q3. That’s welcome, the investor says, but probably not enough to move the shares on its own. So he turns to the balance sheet. Coinbase ended September with $8.6 billion in cash and cash equivalents against $6 billion of long-term debt. None of that debt comes due before 2028, after the company paid off $1.3 billion of convertible notes in June. In his view, that rules out near-term solvency worries, even before counting the company’s crypto holdings.

The cash also funds buybacks. Coinbase repurchased about 7.1 million shares for roughly $1.25 billion in the first nine months and has close to $2 billion of authorization left.

De Silva isn’t trying to time a bitcoin recovery, though he admits the stock still tends to move with it. He doesn’t own any crypto himself, and Coinbase gives him that exposure through the coins it holds on its own books. If bitcoin rallied 50%, he estimates the company’s pre-tax income would get a boost of about $1.1 billion from those holdings alone.

His case doesn’t depend on that happening, though. His base case has bitcoin trading between $65,000 and $80,000 through 2027. In that scenario, spot trading revenue drops about 16% year over year, but derivatives and prediction markets, which have passed $200 million in annualized revenue, make up the difference. He estimates adjusted EBITDA would rise about 28% YoY, with the margin reaching about 30%.

De Silva does point to some risks. Lower rates could reduce stablecoin income, the USDC business leans on a single partner, and a severe crypto crash would be hard to model. Even so, the investor believes Coinbase can grow earnings without a bitcoin rally, and that the market will eventually treat it as part of crypto’s plumbing rather than a stand-in for bitcoin.

All told, he rates COIN a Buy.

On the Street, ANT claims a Strong Buy consensus rating, its $150.50 average price target implying shares will gain 82% over the coming months. COIN is rated a Moderate Buy. At $192.52, its average target points to 12-month returns of 86%. (See ANT stock forecast or COIN stock forecast)

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed in this article are solely those of the featured investor. The content is intended to be used for informational purposes only. It is very important to do your own analysis before making any investment.

data.title: Palantir Stock (PLTR) Has No Room for Error at This Valuation
data.description:
Palantir Technologies, Inc. (PLTR) stock has little room for error at its current valuation, despite the company’s strong growth. The Florida-based software platform developer has lost 8% of its market value so far this year, even after delivering standout Q3 results and raising full-year guidance across key financial metrics. Yet following that pullback, shares still trade at a steep forward P/E multiple of 96x.

Although Palantir’s rapid top-line expansion justifies a premium valuation, a closer look at total contract value (TCV), the international commercial segment, and the earnings sensitivity to certain macro developments suggests the stock is already priced for perfection. For these reasons, I am Bearish on Palantir.

Slow TCV Growth Raises Questions

One of the main reasons behind my Bearish stance on Palantir is the massive gap between TCV growth and revenue growth. In Q3 2026, TCV grew just 6% year-over-year to $2.92 billion, while revenue surged 96% year-over-year to $2.31 billion. Meanwhile, year-over-year TCV growth decelerated sharply from 49% in Q2 when TCV reached $3.37 billion.

At a fundamental level, the disconnect between revenue growth and TCV growth highlights shorter initial contract durations for new contracts. This contrasts with Palantir’s historical operational profile, when the company enjoyed multi-year government contracts. On the Q3 earnings call, CFO David Glazer revealed that several eight-figure contracts were shorter in duration compared to historical averages.

CFO Glazer elaborated that he expects contract durations to eventually increase. “We signed multiple 8-figure deals in the quarter that were shorter in duration than usual, as customers rapidly adopted initial sovereign AI capabilities in their enterprise. It is important to remember that the sovereign AI revolution is only 1 quarter old. As we continue to deliver value with sovereign AI, over time, we expect both the duration and size of these contracts to increase.”

From a valuation perspective, the problem with shorter contract durations is that customers reach renewal or renegotiation dates sooner. Strong revenue conversion today does not automatically lock in multi-year cash flows unless Palantir sustains high retention and expands initial terms at renewal. Slow TCV growth, therefore, highlights this risk faced by the company. I believe Palantir’s valuation multiples will continue to compress in the next few quarters as the market digests this business transition.

International Commercial Segment Is a Slow Compounder

My Bearish stance on Palantir is strengthened by the slower growth seen in international commercial business. In Q3, international commercial revenue grew 21% year-over-year to $184 million. Sequentially, this represented just 1% growth. In comparison, the U.S. commercial business reported 148% year-over-year revenue growth to $984 million in Q3. From a longer-term perspective, the massive gap between U.S. and international growth within the commercial business raises questions about global adoption of Palantir’s products.

Certain macro indicators suggest the global IT spending environment is not supportive of Palantir’s growth. For instance, according to Gartner (IT), European IT spending is expected to reach $1.57 trillion in 2027, with data center systems spending and infrastructure spending expected to emerge as growth hotspots. This indicates global IT budgets are shifting toward compute and infrastructure, which is bad news for application-layer companies such as Palantir.

The regulatory environment in international markets is complicated as well. This presents a challenge for Palantir. In the European Union (EU), companies are expected to comply with the EU Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act, the Cyber Resilience Act, the EU Data Act, and the revised Product Liability Directive. Longer legal reviews, vendor compliance questionnaires, and governance audits slow down pilot-to-production conversion in Europe compared to the United States. Palantir’s adoption, therefore, will be slow and gradual.

U.S. Commercial Growth Mainly Comes from Existing Accounts

Another factor that has contributed to my Bearish stance on Palantir is the customer concentration within its U.S. commercial business. In Q3, Palantir grew U.S. commercial customer count by 29% year-over-year to 686, up just 5% sequentially. This segment’s strong revenue growth was driven by an 88% year-over-year increase in trailing-12-month (TTM) revenue per U.S. commercial customer.

Net dollar retention reached 165% as well. These data points suggest that Palantir’s U.S. commercial growth relies heavily on expanding existing accounts and closing large deals rather than broadening the customer base. If net dollar retention cools from 165% or large account expansions slow, top-line growth will decelerate sharply.

Palantir Is Valued for Perfection

At a forward P/E multiple of 96x, I believe Palantir is valued for flawless execution. That valuation represents a steep premium of more than five times the sector median of 18.2x and well ahead of enterprise software peers such as Datadog (DDOG) at 57.79x and ServiceNow (NOW) at 23.3x.

This is where I believe investing in Palantir exposes investors to a meaningful downside risk. Paying that kind of multiple assumes shorter deal durations and slower bookings growth will not weigh on future revenue recognition. This, however, is a risky assumption that could backfire if revenue growth slows as TCV growth slows. At the same time, international commercial adoption remains a slower growth engine.

I am also wary of the valuation implications of Palantir’s revenue growth relying heavily on existing-account expansion. If net retention moderates, international traction stays muted, or revenue growth decelerates, Palantir’s earnings multiples will compress sharply.

Is Palantir a Buy, According to Wall Street Analysts?

On TipRanks, based on ratings from 25 Wall Street analysts, the average Palantir price target is $229.09, implying 40% upside from the current market price.

Takeaway

Palantir’s stock market performance has been lackluster in 2026. Although the company has continued to grow at a strong pace, its valuation seems to have run ahead of the economic reality it has faced over the past few years. This has led to a valuation multiple compression this year. Looking ahead, I believe there are a few factors that could continue to exert pressure on Palantir’s valuation multiples. For this reason, I am Bearish on Palantir’s prospects.

data.title: Jensen Huang Is Back. Nvidia’s (NVDA) Bull Case Remains
data.description:
Jensen Huang is back at the helm, and Nvidia’s (NVDA) bull case remains in play. Nvidia shares surged 31.5% on November 23 after news of Jensen Huang’s reinstatement, underscoring how closely investor confidence in the company is tied to its co-founder.

While near-term volatility is likely to persist, I remain decisively Bullish over the long term. Nvidia makes the chips, networking gear, and software powering the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, and its earnings story is strong enough to ride out the ups and downs.

Huang’s Return Restores Continuity, but Not Trust

Huang’s return restores strategic continuity, but it does not restore trust overnight. Nvidia disclosed on November 12 that its co-founder and chief executive officer (CEO) had resigned after the board accepted his resignation on November 11. The stock finished that session 4.3% lower. On November 23, Nvidia announced that Huang had been reinstated, and the shares rose 31.5%.

The episode highlighted a degree of key-person risk that I had underestimated. Nvidia’s product cadence and customer confidence have always been closely tied to Huang. His return obviously removes the immediate succession problem. However, it leaves investors with a governance question.

The board reinstated him before completing its independent investigation, shortly after creating a National Security and Export Control Committee on November 17 and alongside launching a search for a Chief Compliance Officer. Those oversight steps are the right moves, but they do not excuse reversing a major leadership decision before the facts are settled.

For my Bullish thesis, Huang’s return is a stabilizer, though stronger governance is still required.

Nvidia’s Earnings Still Point to Powerful AI Demand

Nvidia’s results still point to very strong AI demand, and that’s the part of the argument I find most compelling. Q3 FY2027 revenue was up 103% year-over-year to $115.8 billion, and Data Center revenue was up 110% to $107.6 billion. GAAP diluted earnings per share (EPS) came in at $2.70. Management has guided to around $130 billion in Q4 FY2027 revenue, plus or minus 3%, all the way through the end of the year, despite assuming zero Data Center compute revenue from China.

Nvidia’s product roadmap also gives me confidence the company can sustain growth. The company has started shipping Vera Rubin NVL72, with systems already operating at major cloud partners. This comes as some of its biggest customers continue to invest heavily in AI infrastructure. Meta (META), Google (GOOGL), and Amazon (AMZN) all raised their capital spending plans during their October earnings updates, suggesting that demand for the computing infrastructure Nvidia provides could remain strong.

However, strong demand does not necessarily mean higher profitability. Nvidia expects its Q4 FY2027 gross margin to fall to 71%–72%, from about 75% in Q3 FY2027, as it ramps up its latest products. Competition is also rising, with Google’s tensor processing units (TPUs) and Broadcom’s (AVGO) custom chips offering alternatives to Nvidia’s processors. While these developments deserve attention, I believe Nvidia’s scale and rapid product cadence keep its long-term growth story intact.

NVDA’s Valuation Now Leaves Room for Earnings to Work

Nvidia’s valuation is another reason I remain Bullish. At its November 25 closing price of $149.30, the stock traded at about a 15.52x forward price-to-earnings ratio (P/E), well below the 26.7x recorded at the end of Fiscal Year 2026 and 36.2x at the end of Fiscal Year 2025. The discount looks even more compelling when compared with its peers. AVGO trades at 25.82x forward P/E, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) commands a much higher multiple of 50.24x.

Of course, some discount may be justified given the recent governance concerns. However, I believe the current valuation is becoming hard to ignore, especially considering Nvidia’s market position and continued earnings growth. Nvidia does not need to return to its previous multiples for investors to see meaningful upside over the next year. If earnings continue to meet expectations, the stock has room to recover, which further supports my Buy stance.

What Could Derail My Bullish Thesis?

The biggest risk to my bullish view is that Nvidia’s earnings growth may not meet expectations. If the major tech companies start to scale back their AI infrastructure spend, then we could see weaker demand and margin pressure for Nvidia. Competition from custom AI chips is also still an issue.

Beyond the financials, Jensen Huang’s recent sabbatical and return have highlighted a very real level of key-man risk that I find hard to ignore. His return may have been enough to quell immediate investor angst, but it doesn’t mitigate the governance issues. If those issues continue to fester or start to impact the business, then I would have to reconsider my Buy.

What Is Wall Street Saying About Nvidia?

Turning to Wall Street, Nvidia carries a Strong Buy consensus rating on TipRanks, based on 34 Buys, nine Holds, and one Sell over the past three months. The average analyst price target is $234. Relative to the November 25 closing price of $149.30, that implies about 56.73% upside over the next 12 months.

A recent TipRanks article highlighted the Street’s renewed optimism following Huang’s return. Citi (C) analyst Atif Malik reiterated his Buy rating and raised his price target to $240 from $225, arguing that Huang’s reinstatement removes a major source of uncertainty surrounding Nvidia’s leadership and should help restore confidence in its product roadmap. Goldman Sachs (GS) analyst James Schneider also reaffirmed his Buy rating and maintained a $220 price target.

Conclusion

Wall Street’s Strong Buy consensus, even with analysts flagging ongoing governance overhangs, matches my own view. I’m not predicting the next move in Nvidia’s share price. However, over the next 12-month period, I think the combination of strong earnings power and a sharply compressed valuation more than offsets the governance and geopolitical risks, as long as the business continues to execute.

data.title: 3 Quantum Computing Stocks with over 140% Upside Potential, According to Analysts
data.description:
Analysts remain optimistic about the quantum computing sector, with three stocks offering more than 140% upside potential. These include D-Wave Quantum (QBTS), IonQ (IONQ), and Quantum Computing Inc. (QUBT). TipRanks data shows that all three have positive analyst consensus ratings, with price targets pointing to substantial gains over the next 12 months.

All three stocks rose in Friday’s pre-market trading as buyers returned after steep losses. Over the past month, D-Wave Quantum fell roughly 42%, Quantum Computing Inc. dropped 28%, and IonQ lost about 29%. A rebound across global tech stocks helped lift the group, while optimism around government funding and commercial quantum demand also supported sentiment.

IonQ (IONQ)

IonQ develops quantum computers using trapped-ion technology and continues to expand its customer base.  The company recently reported strong third-quarter results and raised its 2026 revenue outlook. IonQ’s revenue jumped 336% year-over-year to $173.8 million, beating Wall Street estimates. The company also lifted its full-year revenue forecast to $505 million–$515 million, well above its previous outlook. 

Its latest results showed strong demand, with record bookings and higher revenue expectations for 2026. Following the results, Rosenblatt analyst John McPeake maintained a Buy rating and $70 price target. He noted that more customers are buying multiple IonQ products, signaling rising demand. McPeake also said IonQ’s $2 billion October raise gives it ample funds to expand and pursue acquisitions.

Wall Street has a Strong Buy consensus rating on IONQ stock. The average IonQ analyst price target of $57.08 implies 142.50% upside from current levels.

D-Wave Quantum (QBTS)

D-Wave Quantum develops quantum computers and cloud services. It is expanding beyond quantum annealing into gate-model computing. In Q3 2026, revenue rose 21% year over year to $4.5 million. Nine-month bookings jumped 611% to $37.4 million, although quarterly bookings fell 19% to $1.9 million.

The company also launched a beta program for its gate-model quantum simulator and extended its manufacturing deal with SkyWater Technology. It ended the quarter with $503.4 million in cash and marketable securities. Analysts remain bullish, although some have lowered their price targets due to rising costs and near-term margin pressure.

Overall, QBTS carries a Strong Buy consensus rating on TipRanks. The average D-Wave Quantum analyst price target of $26.55 suggests about 279.22% upside from current levels.

Quantum Computing Inc. (QUBT)

Quantum Computing Inc. develops photonic chips and quantum optics systems. It also makes hardware for quantum cybersecurity. In Q3 2026, revenue jumped to $9.5 million from $384,000 a year earlier. Sales from recently acquired photonics and packaging businesses helped drive the increase. Its contract backlog reached $39.1 million, while its net loss widened to $15.1 million due to higher research and operating costs.

The company also made progress on its thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) chip technology and combined its Fab 1 and Fab 2 manufacturing sites. It signed a new pharmaceutical research deal with INmune Bio. QUBT ended the quarter with about $1.3 billion in cash, investments, and accrued interest.

Overall, QUBT carries a Moderate Buy consensus rating on TipRanks. The average QUBT analyst price target of $16.00 suggests about 248.58% upside from current levels.

data.title: Cerebras (CBRS) Expects Revenue to Triple in 2027. Is the Stock a Buy?
data.description:
Cerebras Systems (CBRS) could be the next breakout stock of 2027, with management expecting revenue to triple next year. I rate CBRS a Buy because the market is underpricing Cerebras’ potential to challenge established players in the artificial intelligence (AI) inference market. The wafer-scale AI chipmaker is coming off a strong third quarter, with 70% year-over-year core revenue growth and customer relationships that include Amazon’s (AMZN) cloud unit, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Oracle (ORCL), and Microsoft (MSFT).

Despite that momentum, the stock has been weighed down by recent overhangs, touching a 52-week low of $77.84 on November 5. Now that its initial public offering (IPO) lockup expired on November 10 and its Q3 earnings report is behind it, CBRS looks well-positioned to run higher. Management also noted in its Q3 release that the pipeline for high-speed AI inference grew more than 10x during the quarter.

Cerebras is emerging as a serious challenger to Nvidia (NVDA) as customers prioritize speed and token-generation efficiency. Looking ahead, 2027 is shaping up to be a catalyst-rich year, backed by further details on its Microsoft partnership, up to 700 megawatts of contracted data center capacity coming online through the end of next year, and management’s call for a threefold surge in revenue.

Cerebras Is Built for the AI Inference Era

Cerebras Systems is developing technology built for the next era of AI: Inference. According to Bloomberg Intelligence, this market is expected to grow to $1.3 trillion by 2032, at a compound annual growth rate of 32%. Cerebras established its largest commitment with OpenAI, which contributed about 34%, or $72.4 million, of its latest Q3 revenue.

It has recently secured agreements with three large customers, including AWS, Oracle, and Microsoft.  With commitments from the largest players in the industry, Cerebras has a leg up with its proprietary AI inference technology.

Cerebras’ Wafer-Scale Moat

What differentiates Cerebras from its peers is its wafer-scale architecture, which allows customers to access high-speed computing remotely at speeds well above traditional graphics processing unit (GPU) setups. In its latest Q3 earnings, the company reported that its disaggregated inference approach offers up to five times the throughput per megawatt, enabling more tokens to be generated at a lower cost. That advantage is already showing up in the numbers, with Cloud and Other Services accounting for 63% of Q3 core revenue.

Building on its current CS-4 system, Cerebras is also testing its next-generation Wafer Scale Engine 5 (WSE-5) processor to power the upcoming CS-5. This system is expected to more than double the speed of the CS-4 ahead of an early summer 2027 rollout.

700 Megawatts of Capacity, Mostly Outside the U.S.

With its architectural moat, Cerebras is well positioned to address the data center capacity constraints customers face in the AI industry. Cerebras has secured approximately 700 megawatts of capacity for delivery by the end of 2027. Management has warned that shifting U.S. policies and domestic power constraints could slow stateside builds, so Cerebras is leaning into geographic diversification.

More than 75% of its 2027 data center capacity will come online from outside of the U.S., in Canada, Finland, France, Norway, and other international markets, helping insulate its growth from domestic delays. The international footprint positions Cerebras as a key beneficiary in the AI buildout.

Q3 Results Set Up a Breakout for 2027

Q3 earnings were a turning point for the company and could lead to the stock’s breakout in 2027. Core revenue came in at $230.9 million, up 70% year-over-year, showing that AI inference technology is translating into meaningful revenue growth. One notable area was the growth of its cloud and services revenue segment, which grew 272% year-over-year to $144.9 million. This headline suggests that Cerebras could be a serious alternative to leaders such as Nvidia.  

Along with the headline numbers, guidance for Q4 and full year 2026 look encouraging. Q4 core revenue is expected to be $310 million to $330 million, well above analyst forecasts of $271 million, while Q4 core gross margin is expected to be higher, at 47% to 49%. These expectations set the stage for 2027 and triple revenues in the new year.

CBRS Valuation

With a $21.79 billion market cap and roughly $5.9 billion in net cash, CBRS has an enterprise value of about $15.9 billion and trades at 16.7x management’s 2026 core revenue guidance midpoint of $950 million. If revenue triples in 2027 as projected, that multiple drops to 5.6x, sitting just above Nvidia at 5.3x and well below AMD (AMD) at 6.9x 2027 estimated sales.

Given Cerebras’ much faster projected top-line growth next year, the stock looks attractively priced. However, this is provided management executes on its 700-megawatt capacity rollout and continues marching toward operating profitability.

Is CBRS a Good Stock to Buy?

CBRS has a Strong Buy consensus rating based on nine Buys, zero Holds, and zero Sells assigned in the past three months. On TipRanks, the average CBRS price target of $215.22 implies about 140% upside from the current price. Price targets range from a low of $155 to a Street-high $280 from Barclays.

CBRS Is Emerging as a Leader in AI Inference Stocks

Cerebras enters 2027 as one of the direct ways to invest in AI inference. Its wafer-scale technology has won over AWS, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle. With data center capacity coming online across North America and Europe, the raised guidance points to a strong finish to 2026.

The bull case will ultimately rely on execution, and any delays in the data center capacity could defer revenue growth to later years. Analysts remain bullish on the stock, with Barclays positive on Cerebras’ wafer-scale technology, and customer agreements with AWS and OpenAI contributing to growth.

That said, at 5.6x projected 2027 revenue, I believe the market is underpricing Cerebras’ growth. I rate CBRS a Buy. Key catalysts to watch include Q4 results against guidance, Microsoft deal terms in 2027, and the ramp-up of data centers coming online throughout 2027.

data.title: ‘Finding New Frontiers’: Mizuho Recommends 2 Lesser-Known Space Stocks to Buy
data.description:
Space may be the final frontier, but right now, it is also the expanding frontier of exploration and business – and the two are not as mutually exclusive as the idealists would have us believe. For better or worse, the profit motive is driving the space economy, and an array of companies is moving to establish niches and gain market share. Giants like SpaceX or upstarts like Rocket Lab may be in the lead right now, but they are not the only players on the ‘space board.’

The numbers offer some perspective on the scale of the opportunity. According to a September report from the OECD, global space-related revenues reached an estimated $550 billion to $600 billion in 2025, approaching the size of the semiconductor industry. Meanwhile, private operators accounted for 88% of satellites launched last year, compared with just 23% in 2010, illustrating how much of the activity has shifted toward commercial enterprises.

Smaller companies can frequently offer investors greater upside potential, particularly in an industry undergoing such rapid expansion. They usually focus on more specialized segments, offering unique services or proprietary technology to meet specific customer needs in terms of capability or pricing.

Among those looking beyond the industry’s more familiar names is Mizuho analyst Greg Konrad, who believes investors need to be selective when deciding where to put their money.

“We are bullish on the growth in space, but a bit more selective on the stocks. Space revenue is growing far faster than anything else we cover. Launch is cheap enough that demand is real, the Moon and the defense space domain are adding buyers, and the highest opportunity companies are vertically integrated. The risk is execution and sometimes risk-off as the group itself tends to trade together. Nonetheless we do have to pick winners and sometimes that is the business itself and sometimes it is correlating the business to its valuation. That is somewhat why the divergence in the group,” Konrad opined.

So let’s follow this line of thought and look at two lesser-known space stocks that Konrad believes are worth buying at current levels. Based on the TipRanks database, we’ll also find out whether the rest of Wall Street shares his enthusiasm.

MDA Space, Ltd. (MDA)

We’ll start in the great frozen north, where MDA Space is Canada’s largest developer and manufacturer of space technology. The company is based in Ontario and has been in operation since 1969. Historically, MDA worked in industrial control systems, portable ground stations for satellite monitoring, and high-end radar systems; today, it is known for its work in robotics, satellites, and geointelligence.

MDA has long experience in developing and supporting space infrastructure, from providing supportive technology to NASA’s space shuttle program to independently putting together commercial space robotic technology. The company has also expanded its defense offerings with MDA MIDNIGHT, a spacecraft designed to protect critical assets in orbit.

One of MDA’s most important areas of operation is in satellite communications. The company’s Aurora program is a product line of software-defined digital satellites, offering users the capability to dynamically adjust coverage and bandwidth for increased system flexibility and functionality. MDA supports Aurora by designing and prototyping the necessary ASIC semiconductors in-house, although the large-scale fabrication is sent to third-party foundries.

Space technology is a global domain, and MDA employs more than 4,000 people worldwide, primarily in Canada, the US, the UK, and Israel. The company’s own facility footprint is extensive – it has more than 1 million square feet of floor space for offices, labs, design facilities, and manufacturing lines.

MDA is also pursuing two acquisitions: US-based spacecraft manufacturer Blue Canyon Technologies (BCT) and a majority stake in French satellite data and analytics provider Collecte Localisation Satellites (CLS).

This all adds up to big business, and for 3Q26, MDA reported a work backlog of C$3.9 billion. This is an important metric, providing ‘revenue visibility’ into next year and further on.

In the meantime, MDA generated C$498.1 million in revenue for the third quarter this year, a figure that was up 21.5% year-over-year. The gross profit, at C$125.9 million, was up 16.6% from the year-ago period.

Against this backdrop, Mizuho’s Konrad believes MDA stands out in an industry where commercial opportunities do not necessarily translate into attractive investment propositions.

“MDA is Canada’s national space champion and one of the few highly profitable companies in space, now priming whole constellations on its AURORA software-defined satellites and in-house application specific integrated circuit (ASIC) chips. Blue Canyon Technologies (BCT) adds U.S. defense access, and CLS adds recurring data and analytics. Our thesis rests on three points: 1) total revenue +49% in 2027E, including +11% organic; 2) a C$3.95BB backlog, ~1.8x 2027E total organic revenue, with a C$40BB pipeline behind it; and 3) a 19.0% adjusted EBITDA margin in 2027E with both deals included. We value MDA Space at 18.0x 2028E EBITDA, a ~35% premium to the space/defense tech peer median of 13.3x, reflecting its high margins, growth and M&A catalysts,” Konrad noted.

And just how much money could investors stand to make here? Konrad rates MDA shares an Outperform (i.e., Buy), with a $44 price target implying upside potential of 61.5% from current levels. (To watch Konrad’s track record, click here)

Overall, MDA’s Strong Buy consensus rating is unanimous, based on 11 recent positive analyst reviews. The stock’s current trading price of $27.24 and average target price of $41.35 together indicate a one-year potential gain of ~52%. (See MDA stock forecast)

BlackSky Technology (BKSY)

Now we’ll turn to BlackSky, another company in the field of commercial geospatial intelligence satellites. The company is based in Herndon, Virginia – putting it in close proximity to the US government agencies and Pentagon contractors that are putting a high premium on quality space technology.

BlackSky currently operates a constellation of proprietary satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO), and uses AI-powered software analytics to deliver high-end real-time imagery and insights for a wide range of customers. The company primarily serves US and international government and defense customers, although it also caters to commercial clients.

The company’s customers can tap into BlackSky’s network of satellites and analytics, which promise ‘space-based intelligence at the speed of conflict.’ That’s a vital feature, differentiating BlackSky as a high-end service provider – in today’s fast-paced digital world, yesterday’s information can already be outdated.

BlackSky sets itself apart from the competition by leaning directly into that. Its satellite constellations are ‘high-revisit’ – that is, they consistently make repeat flights over strategic locations, economic assets, and events around the world. Their communications are low-latency, allowing for a fast pace of high- and very-high-resolution imagery, delivered by a first-of-its-kind platform optimized for today’s needs. Customers can receive data, composed of real-time imagery and automated, AI-driven analytics, with an average delivery time of 90 minutes or less.

We should note an important recent move that expands BlackSky’s ability to deliver comprehensive solutions for real-time intelligence on the world’s most important locations with the detail needed to support fast decision-making. Earlier this month, BlackSky announced its acquisition of EpochGeo. EpochGeo is a geospatial data science firm that specializes in artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) solutions from multiple data sources, including RF and signals intelligence, and applies those capabilities in the defense sector. The financial details of the acquisition were not disclosed.

In its 3Q26 report, BlackSky’s revenue hit a company quarterly record of $43 million. This was up 118% year-over-year and beat the forecast by $2.87 million. The company also reached another milestone, reporting its first quarterly operating profit of $405,000. The GAAP diluted EPS came to 10 cents, a sharp turnaround from the 44-cent loss reported for 3Q25, and it beat expectations by 34 cents per share.

While BlackSky’s latest results offer encouragement, Konrad sees reasons to be bullish that extend well beyond the company’s recent financial performance.

“The market under-appreciates how BKSY’s model has evolved from a U.S.-reliant supplier of satellite-based imagery to a global provider of vertically integrated imagery satellite systems and services. This has been driven by the evolution of its enhanced Gen-3 satellite constellation, AROS development, along with its emergence as a seller of the satellite systems themselves. Thesis tied to: 1) Sustainable ~30% revenue growth on an enhanced satellite constellation and a growing satellite prime business; 2) adjusted EBITDA-positive today (15.2% EBITDA margin in 2026E) with a runway to 40.7% margins by 2029E; and 3) a balance sheet that can fund near-term investments,” the analyst wrote.

Konrad backs up his bullish stance with an Outperform (i.e., Buy) rating and a $37 price target that implies about 132% upside from current levels.

All in all, BlackSky’s stock has earned a Strong Buy consensus rating on the Street based on 4 recent analyst reviews, including 3 Buys and 1 Hold. The stock is selling for $15.97 and its $37.13 average target price is practically the same as Konrad’s. (See BKSY stock forecast)

data.title: Rivian vs. Lucid: Which EV Stock Is the Better Buy After Their YTD Plunge?
data.description:
Shares of U.S. electric vehicle maker Rivian (RIVN) are down roughly 50% since the start of the year to about $11.71. Its rival Lucid (LCID) is worse off, with shares down about 76% year-to-date. This comes as both EV makers are still racing to turn a net profit. On Wall Street, analysts are more bullish on Rivian, but Lucid offers the bigger upside of about 128%.

Why Rivian and Lucid Shares Have Sold Off This Year

Rivian shares have sold off this year as the automaker continues to burn cash and post losses. In the third quarter, net loss was $913 million. The EV maker used up $1.12 billion in free cash flow during the quarter.

This took the shine off its revenue, which rose 38% year-over-year to $2.2 billion. Rivian posted record quarterly deliveries of 19,248 units during the period. Demand for the R2, its new and more affordable SUV, drove revenue growth.

Likewise, shares have fallen as its EV credits have dried up due to changes in federal policy. In addition to the R2’s lower prices, this development hurt the automaker’s automotive gross margin in the third quarter.

Notably, Lucid shares also faced pressure amid recent bankruptcy rumors that the company promptly denied.

Why Analysts Like Rivian Better

Analysts are more bullish on Rivian than Lucid. Seaport Global analyst Ronald Jewsikow recently called RIVN stock a Buy. He sees room for the stock to gain beyond Rivian’s planned vehicle lineup. 

Five-star Jefferies analyst Philippe Houchois also recently upgraded Rivian shares from Hold to Buy. He pointed to demand for the R2. According to Houchois, Rivian converted more customer preorders for the high-end R2 launch trim into actual sales than it expected.

By contrast, Jewsikow started coverage of Lucid with a Sell rating. He argued that the EV maker would need significant capital to develop and launch the three new midsize vehicles it is planning.

Meanwhile, four-star Baird analyst Ben Kallo recently maintained his Hold rating on Lucid. However, Kallo noted that Lucid’s efforts to reduce expenses are beginning to show results. He also pointed to the carmaker’s progress in developing its self-driving technology.

Which EV Stock Is the Better Buy?

As mentioned earlier, Rivian (RIVN) has the better consensus analyst rating: a Moderate Buy. However, TipRanks’ Stock Comparison tool shows that Lucid (LCID) offers the bigger upside of about 128%.

data.title: ‘It Isn’t Coming,’ Says Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) investors barely had time to enjoy some respite. Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Nov. 23, and chip stocks ripped higher on the news. The memory maker then handed back almost all of that gain over the next two sessions, after BNP Paribas downgraded the stock to Neutral and TrendForce trimmed its 2027 memory forecasts on order cuts from Chinese cloud providers.

U.S. markets are closed today for Thanksgiving, so the shares sit at Wednesday’s close of $601.25, roughly half their June 25 record close of $1,213.56.

So, where to now for this this until-recently high-flying stock? Well, according to a top investor using the pseudonym The Asian Investor (TAI), the market has this one wrong. In TAI’s view, the selling has been driven by doubts about the AI boom and about debt-funded spending by neocloud providers, not by anything going wrong inside Micron’s business. The valuation now reflects a level of gloom that the fundamentals don’t support.

Micron trades at about 3.4x forward earnings, and peers SK hynix and Sandisk are even cheaper at roughly 2x to 2.5x. According to TAI, multiples this low only make sense if investors expect profits to slump within the next two or three years. The investor doesn’t see that happening and argues the current price leaves plenty of room for error.

The case rests on high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the chips that sit beside AI processors in data centers. TrendForce expects HBM to take up about 30% of the industry’s DRAM wafer capacity in 2027, up from around 22% this year. Every wafer that goes to HBM is one less for regular DRAM, which keeps supply tight across the board. TrendForce also projects that blended HBM prices will rise 121% year over year in 2027. Micron says much of its 2027 HBM supply is already spoken for, at prices well above this year’s, and it is scaling up HBM4 production. TAI, who ranks among the top 4% of investors on TipRanks, adds that agentic AI tools need far more memory than earlier AI workloads, which could stretch the shortage out for years.

The next test is the fiscal first-quarter report on Dec. 17. Wall Street expects adjusted EPS of about $38.20, compared with $4.78 a year earlier, a jump of roughly 700% YoY, and analysts have been raising their estimates ahead of the release.

The main risk, in TAI’s view, is that the HBM boom fades the way memory cycles usually do. If AI spending stalls, Micron would have to accept lower prices for its DRAM and HBM, and its gross margin would shrink with them. For now, the investor sees hyperscalers raising their capital budgets while their sales keep growing, which suggests the AI spending is paying off. Micron’s own management expects supply to be tighter in 2027 and 2028 than it is now.

“With a positive earnings trend, leading gross profit growth (on a TTM basis) in the industry group, triple-digit earnings growth, and a favorable EPS estimate revision trend three weeks before earnings, I see not only a strong earnings report but also a major revaluation catalyst ahead for investors,” the 5-star investor summed up.

Accordingly, TAI has made Micron the biggest memory bet in the portfolio and rates the stock a Strong Buy. (To watch TAI’s track record, click here)

That is also the conclusion reached by the analyst consensus, a rating based on 28 Buys and 2 Holds. Going by the $1,574 average price target, a year from now, shares will be changing hands for a 162% premium. (See MU stock forecast)

data.title: SpaceX vs. Rocket Lab: One Space Stock Is a Buy, the Other Isn’t Worth the Price, Says Mizuho
data.description:
Getting a satellite into orbit has never been cheaper, but owning the companies that put them there has cost investors plenty this year. SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) and Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) both ran hard into SpaceX’s June IPO and have spent much of the time since handing those gains back. Space stocks still move as a pack, so a rough day for one usually drags the rest along.

Wednesday showed how jumpy the trade is. SpaceX opened sharply lower on Wednesday and at one point was down about 9% from Tuesday’s close as the cost of insuring its debt hit a record and investors pushed back on a possible tie-up with Tesla. It recovered after the FCC approved its plan for up to 1 million satellites working as orbital data centers, closing at $127.44, about 37% below its June record close. Rocket Lab ended the day at $47.02, roughly 69% off its May peak, with the first flight of its Neutron rocket now pushed into 2027. U.S. markets are closed today for Thanksgiving.

Mizuho analyst Greg Konrad recently launched coverage of the space sector and is upbeat on the industry, but he thinks the theme alone isn’t enough. What matters, in his view, is whether a company delivers and what investors are paying for it.

SpaceX

Konrad sees SpaceX as the best example in the group of a company that does everything in-house. Reusable rockets have brought its launch costs down by roughly 85% to 90% compared with the historical average, and everything else is built on that cheap ride. Falcon and Starship carry Starlink satellites into orbit, Starlink brings in the money, and the AI arm, built around xAI and the Colossus compute clusters, is where the analyst sees the biggest potential payoff.

Starlink is the part that’s already proven. It generated $11.4 billion in revenue in 2025 at an adjusted EBITDA margin of about 63%. The next step is the V3 satellite, which Konrad says puts about 20 times as much bandwidth into orbit on each launch. That should let Starlink go after crowded cities that older satellites couldn’t serve well. V3s fly on Starship, which reached orbit for the first time on Sept. 28 and released 26 of them.

The growth Konrad is modeling is enormous: revenue up 201% year over year in 2027, with AI revenue up 315%, connectivity up 70% and the space business up 54%.

The flip side to that is spending. Heavy investment in AI and Starship has pushed free cash flow below zero even as EBITDA grows. He also flags Starship’s timeline, the cost of the AI buildout, governance, and the flood of shares coming out of lockup, with the final IPO tranche unlocking on Dec. 8. Still, Konrad thinks owning the rockets, the network and the compute gives SpaceX an edge no one else can match.

“SpaceX is the ultimate vertical integration play,” he said, rating the stock as Outperform. His $205 price target implies shares will gain 61% in the months ahead. (To watch Konrad’s track record, click here)

Most of Konrad’s colleagues agree with that stance. With an additional 27 Buys, 6 Holds and 1 Sell, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. At $265, the average price target implies shares will gain 108% over the 12-month timeframe. (See SPCX stock forecast)

Rocket Lab

Rocket Lab is a tougher call for Konrad, and the business isn’t the reason. He likes the company, and of the space names he covers, it has the clearest view of future revenue.

That is contingent on three things happening: more frequent Electron launches, Neutron’s planned ramp from one flight to three and then five a year, and a Space Systems unit that is graduating from selling parts to leading whole spacecraft programs. Space Systems already brought in about two-thirds of 2025 revenue. The pending Iridium deal, expected to close by mid-2027, would add a fourth leg of recurring revenue, though Konrad doesn’t expect the bigger synergies until after 2030.

Demand isn’t the issue either. Few companies can reliably reach orbit, launch slots are scarce, and the backlog hit an all-time high of $3.57 billion at the end of September.

The sticking point is valuation. Konrad expects revenue to grow 29% in 2027 and 36% in 2028, which puts Rocket Lab right around the middle of the space group. Yet on forward revenue, the stock is valued at a steep premium to its peers, SpaceX included.

Investors, in other words, are already paying for growth he sees as fairly average. With Neutron’s debut slipping and Iridium’s biggest payoff not due until the next decade, there isn’t much room for error.

“We like the business, but struggle with the valuation,” Konrad said. He values the shares at 10.5 times 2028 pro forma EV/revenue and rates Rocket Lab as Underperform (i.e., Sell) with a $40 price target. That figure implies shares will fall another 15% over the next year.

Konrad, however, is the Street’s lone RKLB bear. Elsewhere, an additional 15 Buys and 3 Holds all add up to a Moderate Buy consensus view. The forecast calls for 12-month returns of 96%, given the average price target clocks in at $92.33. (See RKLB stock forecast)

U.S. markets are closed for Thanksgiving on Thursday, a break for Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) shareholders after another rough session. The flash memory maker fell again on Wednesday after TrendForce said demand for NAND chips in China looks even weaker than it had thought. Chinese cloud companies can’t get enough GPUs, so they need less of the storage that goes with them. That followed the research firm’s warning last week that NAND contract prices will start falling early next year.

Sandisk closed Wednesday at $73.61, down about 5.5% on the day. The stock has more than halved over the past month and sits about 75% below its June 25 record close, adjusted for the 8-for-1 stock split that took effect last week.

The latest 13F filings, which show holdings as of Sept. 30, reveal that most big investors were buying. Sandisk had fallen about 23% during the third quarter, and many funds used the drop to add shares. The share counts below are from before the split.

The largest single move, though, was a sale. Leopold Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness sold all 2.5 million of its Sandisk shares. At the end of June, that stake was worth $5.67 billion, the fund’s biggest holding at 28% of the stocks it reported. The fund kept some exposure through call options with a notional value of $183 million. The sale was part of a forced unwind after July’s AI selloff hit the heavily leveraged fund with margin calls. Stanley Druckenmiller’s Duquesne Family Office also sold out, unloading 34,900 shares worth about $79 million at the end of June.

Jericho Capital made the biggest purchase, opening a stake of 391,880 shares worth $682 million on Sept. 30. Renaissance Technologies increased its position more than 55-fold, from 4,980 shares to 276,460, worth $481 million. GQG Partners opened a $210 million stake, Brad Gerstner’s Altimeter Capital started a smaller position of 25,170 shares, and Bridgewater Associates went from just 317 shares to 66,756, worth about $116 million.

By 13Foresight’s count, 1,192 funds opened or added to Sandisk positions in the quarter, against 870 that trimmed or sold out. Any of them that held on are sitting on steep losses, since the stock is now about two-thirds below its Sept. 30 price. The filings don’t show whether they’ve sold since.

On the Street, the NAND flash specialist still gets plenty of support. Based on 12 Buys and 3 Holds, the analyst consensus rates the stock a Strong Buy. At $252.06, the average price target implies shares will gain 242% in the months ahead. (See SNDK stock forecast)

data.title: 3 Vanguard Sector ETFs That Give Investors an Edge
data.description:
Vanguard offers a wide range of sector ETFs that give investors exposure to different parts of the U.S. stock market. Some focus on steady demand for everyday products and the energy sector, while others target technology companies with strong growth potential. Using TipRanks’ Best Vanguard ETFs tool, three Vanguard ETFs stand out: Vanguard Energy ETF (VDE), Vanguard Consumer Staples ETF (VDC), and Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT).

VDE invests in energy companies, VDC focuses on consumer staples companies, while VGT holds major technology stocks.

According to TipRanks’ unique ETF Analyst Consensus, which is based on a weighted average of analyst ratings for each ETF’s holdings, VGT has a Strong Buy rating. Based on analysts’ price targets, VGT’s average price target of $150.69 offers the highest upside of over 45%. It invests in tech companies that are growing fast. These companies also benefit from rising demand for AI and cloud services.

Meanwhile, VDC and VDE carry Moderate Buy ratings. VDE offers upside of 24%, and VDC offers 7%. Energy stocks are sensitive to changes in oil and gas prices, while consumer staples companies generally see slower growth due to steady demand for everyday products.

Vanguard Consumer Staples ETF (VDC)

The Vanguard Consumer Staples ETF (VDC) invests in consumer defensive companies. These companies sell everyday essentials like food, beverages, and household goods. Because demand for these products stays steady even during economic slowdowns, VDC is often seen as a defensive ETF with lower volatility. It has a beta of 0.25.

The fund has 95.4% of its holdings in the consumer defensive sector. It also offers a dividend yield of 1.94% with a quarterly dividend of $1.21 per share.

VDC owns 105 stocks with total assets of $8.3 billion. Its top holdings include major consumer brands such as Walmart (WMT), Costco Wholesale (COST), and Procter & Gamble (PG).

Vanguard Energy ETF (VDE)

The Vanguard Energy ETF (VDE) offers broad exposure to the U.S. energy sector. VDE holds stocks involved in oil and gas exploration, production, refining, equipment services, and midstream infrastructure. The ETF has historically performed well when oil prices rise and can also help protect against inflation.

The fund has 99.19% of its holdings in the energy sector. VDE has historically offered a higher dividend yield than the broader market. VDE has a dividend yield of 2.31% and pays a $1.05 quarterly dividend.

Its top 3 holdings are Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM), Chevron (CVX), and ConocoPhillips (COP). Overall, VDE holds 113 stocks with total assets worth $9.93 billion.

Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT)

Vanguard Information Technology ETF is focused solely on U.S. technology stocks, with major holdings including Nvidia (NVDA), Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT), Broadcom (AVGO), and Micron (MU). The ETF has 99.38% of its holdings in the technology sector. VGT has 316 stocks with total assets of $133.08 billion.

The fund’s narrow focus can lead to bigger swings than broader market funds. With a beta of 1.49, the ETF tends to be more volatile, and its expense ratio of 0.09% is slightly higher than some diversified alternatives.

data.title: SpaceX vs. Tesla: What Sets Them Apart, and Could They Merge?
data.description:
Elon Musk leads two companies with very different goals. SpaceX (SPCX) builds rockets and runs an internet service from space, while Tesla (TSLA) makes electric cars and sells power storage systems. Each has its own path to growth, but a possible merger has raised new questions for investors.

The prospect of a merger has drawn fresh interest. On November 24, the Financial Times reported that Tesla and SpaceX had named five board members to lead talks. The report said the firms were looking at a possible $3.5 trillion all-stock deal. The two firms have yet to announce a deal, and the terms remain open.

SpaceX: A Leader in Space and Satellite Internet

SpaceX has built its name by launching rockets and sending gear into space. The company also builds Starship, a large rocket meant to carry heavy loads into space. SpaceX also won the first U.S. approval to launch up to 1 million satellites for AI data centers in space.

Starlink, its satellite web service, is a key source of cash. Reusable rockets have cut launch costs by 85% to 90%, while Starlink had $11.4 billion in 2025 sales and 10.3 million users.

Recently, Mizuho Securities analyst Brett Linzey started coverage of SpaceX with a Buy rating and $205 price target. He sees growth in space, Starlink and AI, but flags high costs, Starship delays and risks tied to future share sales.

Tesla: More Than an EV Company?

Tesla is best known for its electric vehicles, such as the Model 3 and Model Y. It also sells home and grid power storage systems. Its main car unit faces stiff price pressure as more companies enter the EV market. Tesla is also investing millions into self-driving technology, AI, and robots.

Seaport Global analyst Ronald Jewsikow began coverage of Tesla with a Buy rating and a $475 price target. He sees robotaxis as the main source of future growth and expects annual sales to reach $3 billion to $4 billion by the end of 2027. Jewsikow also expects car sales and margins to rise in 2027. While Alphabet’s (GOOGL) Waymo remains his pick for market lead in 2030, he sees scope for Tesla to gain ground.

Could SpaceX and Tesla Merge?

A Tesla-SpaceX merger would raise key questions about the value of each company, the share swap terms, and who would hold control. Tesla shareholders could gain exposure to space and satellite web services, but they would also take on the costs and risks of those businesses.

RBC Capital analyst Ken Herbert sees a merger as a real chance by early 2027, sooner than he had expected. He also said Tesla may get a price above its fair value, but some investors may accept a deal without a large premium. Herbert reiterated his Buy ratings on both companies.

Which Stock Does Wall Street Prefer?

According to TipRanks Stock Comparison Tool, SpaceX currently has a Strong Buy consensus rating while Tesla has a Moderate Buy. SpaceX’s average analyst price target implies a higher upside of nearly 108%, compared with 8% for Tesla.

data.title: 3 High-Yield Dividend Stocks to Watch This Thanksgiving
data.description:
Thanksgiving is a good time to review income investments through Dividend Stocks. Three stocks stand out for their high yields: Frontline (FRO), Nordic American Tankers (NAT), and Ares Capital (ARCC). All three pay dividends, but their income profiles differ. Based on TipRanks data, their indicated yields range from about 10% to 13%.

Frontline (FRO)

Frontline operates oil tankers, transporting crude oil and petroleum products. Its earnings depend heavily on shipping rates, which can rise or fall quickly.

The company has a record of quarterly dividends, but payments have varied widely. Its latest declared regular quarterly dividend is $2.38 per share, reflecting a current yield of 12.97%. In 2025, regular quarterly dividends totaled just $0.93, highlighting the risk of relying on peak-cycle payouts.

TipRanks reports a Moderate Buy consensus rating on FRO. The average analyst price target of $58.07 implies 21.9% upside from the November 25 closing price of $47.65.

Nordic American Tankers (NAT)

Nordic American Tankers operates a fleet of Suezmax oil tankers. Its business is exposed to the same freight-rate cycle as Frontline.

NAT paid a dividend of $0.27 per share in its latest reported quarter, implying a current yield of 12.19%. The company has paid quarterly dividends, but the amounts have changed significantly. For example, payments rose from $0.10 in September 2025 to $0.27 in September 2026.

On TipRanks, NAT has a Hold consensus rating with an average analyst price target of $8.50 implying 31.2% upside from the November 25 closing price.

Ares Capital (ARCC)

Ares Capital is a U.S. specialty finance company that lends money to mid-sized businesses. It is not a traditional bank or an asset management company. Its income comes largely from its investment portfolio rather than shipping rates.

ARCC has maintained a $0.48 quarterly dividend throughout 2024, 2025, and 2026. That equals $1.92 annually, with a yield of 10.13%. Its dividend record is more stable than those of the tanker companies, although credit losses could still affect future payments.

On TipRanks, ARCC has a Strong Buy consensus rating with the average analyst price target of $20.42 implying 7.7% upside from the November 25 closing price.

data.title: 3 Space Stocks with 95%+ Upside Potential, According to Analysts
data.description:
Growth stocks can offer strong returns as their businesses expand. Planet Labs (PL), Rocket Lab (RKLB), and Intuitive Machines (LUNR) stand out for their upside potential. Based on analysts’ average price targets, LUNR leads with over 188% upside, followed by PL at 182% and RKLB at 96%.

A growth stock is a company whose sales and earnings are expected to grow faster than the broader market. Investors buy growth stocks mainly for share-price gains.

Planet Labs (PL)

Planet Labs uses satellites to take images of Earth. It sells this data to businesses and governments for tasks such as mapping, farming, and defense. The company is expanding its business to meet rising demand for satellite images and data. It is also investing in new satellite technology and AI tools that could open up new ways to make money. However, PL stock is down more than 45% year-to-date.

Analysts have rated Planet Labs’ stock as a Moderate Buy, backed by eight Buys and three Holds assigned in the last three months. Meanwhile, PL’s average stock price target of $30.0 suggests a potential upside of over 180% from current levels.

Intuitive Machines (LUNR)

Intuitive Machines builds lunar landers and provides services for NASA and other customers. It is considered a growth stock because it aims to expand its business through more Moon missions and new space contracts. However, its growth depends on mission success and winning new deals.

LUNR stock has a Strong Buy rating based on eight Buys and one Sell assigned in the last three months. LUNR stock’s average price target of $26.33 implies an upside potential of over 185%.

Rocket Lab (RKLB)

Rocket Lab builds rockets and spacecraft and provides launch services. Its reusable medium-lift rocket, Neutron, is expected to launch in 2027 and could be a key catalyst for the stock. Its planned acquisition of Iridium (IRDM) could also give the company a larger revenue base.

Analysts have rated RKLB stock a Moderate Buy, based on 15 Buys, three Holds, and one Sell assigned in the past three months. Rocket Lab’s average price target of $92.33 points to a potential upside of 96% from current levels.
